title: Hilary of Poitiers (13 January)
hookLine: a married convert who searched his way into the Church, then took exile rather than sign

cards: A grown man in Roman Gaul, comfortable, educated, with a household of his own, sits with his books and a question that won't leave him alone: what is a human life for? He has tried the philosophers.
Eat well, rest well, live decently. It isn't enough. Then he opens the Jewish scriptures and reaches the burning bush, where Moses asks God's name and hears an answer that is barely a name at all.
As a bishop, he will call that moment the turn of his life. His name was Hilary, and he would choose exile over a signature.

teach.h: I AM WHO AM: A CONVERT'S TURNING POINT.
teach.b: Hilary tells his own story at the start of his book On the Trinity. God's words to Moses stopped him. In the Douay-Rheims: "I AM WHO AM."
Nothing, he writes, could say more about God than that: God simply is. He read on into the Gospels and asked for baptism. Tradition says he already had a wife and a daughter.

Later the people of Poitiers made this married convert their bishop. Then the argument arrived. Christians were fighting over whether the Son is truly God, as fully as the Father, or something a step lower.
The Emperor favored the bishops who said a step lower, and leaned on the rest to go along and to condemn Athanasius, the bishop of Alexandria who held that the Son is fully God.

teach.h: HE WOULD NOT SIGN, SO HE WAS EXILED.
teach.b: Hilary would not put his name to it.

teach.h: IN EXILE HE WROTE ON THE TRINITY.
teach.b: So he was sent far to the east, into exile. And there, cut off from his church, he wrote.

teach.h: IN THE NAME OF THE FATHER, AND OF THE SON, AND OF THE HOLY GHOST.
teach.b: On the Trinity starts from the words of baptism, at the close of Matthew's Gospel: "baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost."
His point is simple and stubborn: if that is the name you were baptized into, you don't get to quietly edit it later. Later he came home and kept teaching.

Tradition says a man just out of the army came to learn from him, the one the Church remembers as Martin of Tours. The Church later named Hilary a Doctor of the Church. Steady, here, doesn't mean loud.
It means the same answer on a good day and in exile.

how: Catholics keep Hilary's memorial in January with the Mass and the Liturgy of the Hours, honoring him as a bishop and Doctor of the Church whose writing on the Trinity is still read.

o: a monk who translated the Bible into Latin
a convert bishop exiled for refusing to sign

games.q: Hilary of Poitiers — tap the pairs.
p: the book he wrote in exile
the bishop he would not condemn
an ex-soldier who came to learn from him

s: Hilary was raised a Christian from birth
he came to the faith as an adult, through reading, and asked for baptism.
Hilary wrote On the Trinity while in exile
sent away for refusing to sign, he wrote it far from his church.
Hilary signed the condemnation to keep his post
he refused, and was exiled for it.

games.q: you're Hilary, a bishop. the Emperor's party wants your name on a condemnation of Athanasius. sign, and you keep your church. what do you do?
o: sign, and keep serving your people.
games.why: he refused and was sent into exile. there he wrote On the Trinity, and later came home to Poitiers.

practice: Bring to mind someone whose name gets handled carelessly when they aren't in the room, and instead of rehearsing the gossip, find one true, good sentence about them you could say out loud.
If you pray, hold that person before God; if you don't, keep their face in mind until the sentence feels steady.

wordCard.voice: Hilary. A convert and married man made bishop of Poitiers, who chose exile over condemning a fellow bishop, and wrote On the Trinity far from home.

orig.note: Latin: Hilary's name as he wrote it; his books are in Latin.

carryVoice: Your line: hilary the steady. Tomorrow, a young man who walks out into the desert. See you then.
